name: AI for Seniors: Using AI Assistants
objectives: Given a list of everyday tasks, identify which tasks an AI assistant can help with and which need a doctor, a bank or another person, getting at least 4 of 5 right
Using your phone, tablet or computer, open a free AI assistant from its official app store or website and find the message box or microphone, without help
Given a real need from your own life, write or say a prompt that gives what you need, your situation and how you want the answer, so the first answer is useful

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What an AI assistant is
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Say in your own words what an AI assistant can and cannot do for you.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of everyday tasks, you will identify which tasks an AI assistant can help with and which need a doctor, a bank or another person, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
An AI assistant is a computer program you can talk to or type to in everyday words, as if you were writing a note to a helpful neighbor. You ask a question, and a few seconds later it writes an answer.
Well-known free assistants include ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini. They are good at explaining things simply, writing a first draft of a card or letter, giving ideas for a hobby, and making lists.
An assistant is not a person, and it is not your doctor, lawyer or bank. It does not know you, and it can be wrong even when it sounds very sure. You are in charge: you decide what to ask and what to believe.
Words to know:
- AI: short for artificial intelligence: computer programs that can do tasks like writing or answering questions.
- AI assistant: an AI program you chat with by typing or speaking.
Try it now: On a piece of paper, write three things an AI assistant could help you with this month, for example a card for a grandchild, a question about a garden plant, or a recipe.
You can now say what an AI assistant is, name three ways it could help you, and explain why you still check what it says.

check.q: Which task is an AI assistant good at?
options: Writing a first draft of a birthday card
Giving you your blood test results
Going to the doctor for you
check.why: Assistants are good at drafts, ideas and lists; they are not your doctor or bank.

check.q: An AI assistant sounds very sure about a rule for your benefits. What do you do?
options: Trust it because it sounds sure
Remember that it can be wrong, and check with the office
Ask it to promise it is right
check.why: Assistants can be wrong even when they sound sure, and you decide what to believe.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Opening an assistant on your phone, tablet or computer
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Open a free AI assistant and find the box where you type or speak.
This lesson builds toward: Using your phone, tablet or computer, you will open a free AI assistant from its official app store or website and find the message box or microphone, without help.
You can use an assistant on a smartphone, a tablet or a computer. Choose the device you feel most comfortable with. A grandchild, friend or library helper can sit with you the first time.
On a phone or tablet: open the app store (the Play Store on Android, the App Store on iPhone and iPad). Tap the search box, type the assistant's name, and install the app made by the real company: OpenAI for ChatGPT, Microsoft for Copilot, Google for Gemini.
On a computer: open your web browser and type the address carefully, for example chatgpt.com, copilot.microsoft.com or gemini.google.com. Some let you start without an account; others ask you to sign in.
Look for the message box, usually near the bottom of the screen. It often says "Ask anything" or "Message". Many apps also show a small microphone you can tap to speak instead of typing.
Step by step:
- Pick your phone, tablet or computer.
- Phone or tablet: install the official app from the app store. Computer: type the web address in the browser.
- Find the message box near the bottom of the screen.
- Find the microphone button if you would rather speak.
Words to know:
- App store: the official place on a phone or tablet to get apps safely.
- Web browser: the program you use to visit websites, such as Chrome, Edge or Safari.
- Microphone button: a small picture of a microphone you tap to speak instead of type.
Try it now: Open one free assistant. Find the message box and type, or say: Hello, I am new to this. Please answer in short, simple sentences. Read its reply.
You can now open a free AI assistant and find where to type or speak your question.

check.q: Who makes the real Microsoft Copilot app?
options: Any company with a similar name
check.why: Install the app made by the real company: Microsoft for Copilot.

check.q: You find typing hard on your phone. What do you look for in the assistant app?
options: The small microphone you can tap to speak
check.why: Many apps show a microphone so you can speak instead of typing.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Asking a clear question
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write or say a question that gets a useful answer the first time.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real need from your own life, you will write or say a prompt that gives what you need, your situation and how you want the answer, so the first answer is useful.
What you type or say to an assistant is called a prompt. The clearer the prompt, the better the answer.
A good prompt has three parts: what you need, a little about your situation, and how you want the answer. For example: "My granddaughter turns 8 on Saturday and loves horses. Write a short birthday message from Grandma. Use simple words."
A prompt that is too short, like "birthday", makes the assistant guess, and you get a general answer. It is fine to write a few sentences. Take your time; the assistant waits for you.
Step by step:
- Say what you need.
- Add a little about your situation, with no private details.
- Say how you want the answer: short, simple words, large steps, or a list.
Words to know:
- Prompt: what you type or say to an AI assistant to ask for something.
Try it now: Pick one item from your list in Lesson 1. Write a prompt with all three parts, send it, and read the answer slowly.
You can now ask an AI assistant a clear question with what you need, your situation and how you want the answer.

options: What you type or say to the assistant
check.why: A prompt is your request to the assistant, typed or spoken.

check.q: You want a thank-you note for your neighbor who fixed your fence. Which prompt is best?
options: "My neighbor fixed my fence. Write a short, warm thank-you note in simple words."
check.why: It says what you need, your situation and how you want the answer.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Asking for a simpler or shorter answer
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Use follow-up questions to make an answer easier to read and use.
This lesson builds toward: Given an answer that is too long or hard to read, you will ask follow-up requests, one at a time, to make it simpler or shorter, until it is easy for you to read and use.
You never have to accept the first answer. The assistant remembers what you said earlier in the same chat, so you can ask it to change its answer.
Helpful follow-ups: "Please use simpler words." "Make it shorter." "Put it in numbered steps." "Explain step 3 again." "Give me an example." "Make it sound warmer."
If you have trouble reading small text, you can also make the text bigger on your device. Ask a family member to show you the text size setting, or ask the assistant: "How do I make the text bigger on my iPhone?"
Step by step:
- Read the first answer slowly.
- Decide what would make it better.
- Ask for that one change.
- Repeat until the answer works for you.
Words to know:
- Follow-up: a second question that builds on the answer you got.
Try it now: Take the answer from Lesson 3. Ask for two changes, one at a time, such as "make it shorter" and then "make it sound warmer". Compare the first and last answers.
You can now improve an AI answer by asking clear follow-up questions.

check.q: Why can you ask the assistant to change its answer?
options: It remembers what you said earlier in the same chat
It has to start over each time
check.why: In the same chat the assistant remembers earlier messages, so you can ask for changes.

check.q: A recipe answer is one long paragraph. What do you send next?
check.why: A clear follow-up that names the change makes the answer easier to use.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Checking an answer before you act on it
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check an AI answer with a trusted source before you rely on it.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI answer about health, money, a phone number or a date, you will check the fact with an official website, your doctor or pharmacist, or a person you trust, before you act on it.
AI assistants sometimes make things up: a wrong phone number, a store hour, a medicine fact or a rule that has changed. This is called a hallucination.
Always check anything about your health, medicines, money, benefits such as Social Security or Medicare, dates, addresses and phone numbers. Check with the official website, the office itself, your doctor or pharmacist, or a person you trust.
A good habit is to ask: "Where can I check this?" Then find that official page yourself. Official United States government websites end in .gov.
Step by step:
- Find the facts in the answer: numbers, dates, names, rules.
- Look them up on the official website or call the office.
- If they do not match, trust the official source.
- For health and money, also ask your doctor, pharmacist or a person you trust.
Words to know:
- Hallucination: when an AI writes something that sounds true but is made up.
- .gov: the ending of official United States government website addresses.
Try it now: Ask an assistant for the opening hours of your local library. Then check the library's own website or call it. Did the answer match?
You can now spot facts that need checking and check them with a trusted source.

check.q: What is a hallucination in AI?
options: When the assistant speaks out loud
When the assistant makes up something that sounds true
check.why: AI can make up a wrong phone number, store hour or rule that sounds real.

check.q: The assistant tells you how much of a medicine to take. What do you do?
options: Check with your doctor or pharmacist first
check.why: Health and medicine answers must be checked with your doctor or pharmacist.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Keeping your private information safe
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use an AI assistant without sharing private information.
This lesson builds toward: When you write a prompt or get an urgent call or message, you will keep private information out and spot the warning signs of a scam, sharing no private numbers, passwords or codes.
Never type private information into an AI assistant: your Social Security number, Medicare number, bank or card numbers, passwords, or full home address. You can get the help you need without them. Write "[my number]" instead.
Scammers use AI too. They can write convincing messages and can even copy the voice of a grandchild on the phone. Be careful with any call or message that rushes you, asks for money or gift cards, or asks for a code sent to your phone.
If something feels wrong, stop. Hang up, and call the person back on a number you already know is real.
Step by step:
- Before you send a prompt, read it for private information.
- Replace it with a placeholder like "[my number]".
- Treat rushing, gift cards and code requests as warning signs.
- Call back on a number you already know.
Words to know:
- Private information: details that could let someone pretend to be you or take your money.
- Placeholder: a stand-in word like "[my number]" used instead of the real detail.
Try it now: Final task: ask an assistant for an easy recipe for four people, ask it to put the steps in short numbered lines, ask one follow-up question, and check one fact, such as a cooking temperature, on a trusted website or with someone you trust.
You can now use an AI assistant for a real task, check its answer, and keep your private information safe.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Opened the assistant Needed someone else to open the assistant, or used an unofficial app or site. Opened an official assistant and found the message box or microphone. Can show a friend or family member how to open it. Clear request The prompt is vague, for example "recipe". Asked for an easy recipe for four people, with the situation and how the answer should look. Added a detail such as a food someone cannot eat, and the first answer was close to ready. Made it easier Used the first answer as it was, even if it was hard to read. Asked for short numbered steps and one more follow-up question. Asked for changes one at a time and can say what each one fixed. Fact checked Trusted a fact such as a cooking temperature without checking. Checked one fact on a trusted website or with a person they trust. Can say where they checked it and whether it matched. Private information kept out The prompt includes a private number, address or password. No private information in any prompt. Can name two scam warning signs. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which of these should you never type into an AI assistant?
options: The name of a bird you saw
check.why: Medicare, Social Security and bank numbers are private; use a placeholder instead.

check.q: A text says your account will close today unless you send the code you just got. What do you do?
options: Do not share the code; call the company on a number you know
check.why: Rushing you and asking for a code are warning signs of a scam.
